name: Ampakines (CX717, etc.)
lead: Ampakines are a class of experimental drugs that strengthen the brain's AMPA glutamate receptors, the receptors responsible for fast excitatory signalling. They are discussed in nootropic and focus communities as memory, alertness and cognition enhancers, which people link to sharper study, work and training performance. The best-known members are CX516, CX717, CX1739 and farampator (Org 24448) [2][1].

They act as positive allosteric modulators: they slow the closing of the AMPA channel after glutamate binds, prolonging the signal without activating the receptor themselves [2][2]. The compounds were developed from the 1990s by Cortex Pharmaceuticals, and none has been approved as a medicine [2][3].

Human studies include CX516 added to antipsychotics in schizophrenia, CX516 in mild cognitive impairment, farampator in healthy elderly volunteers, and a 2025 phase 2a trial of CX717 in adult ADHD [4][5][6][7][8]. CX717 also reversed opioid-induced breathing depression in volunteers in work described in reviews [9][2].

Development has been held by a small number of companies. Cortex Pharmaceuticals, later renamed RespireRx in 2015, was the main developer, and regulators have at times halted or restricted CX717 trials.[25][26]

angle.text: Ampakines attract people seeking better focus, memory and alertness for studying, work and training. They remain investigational research compounds.

paras: Ampakines are a subgroup of AMPA receptor positive allosteric modulators, mostly with a benzamide or closely related structure, and the CX-prefixed compounds come from the Cortex programme.[25] Early compounds included CX516, CX546 and CX614; later ones include CX691 (farampator), CX717, CX1739 and others.[25] CX1739 is reported to be roughly five times as potent as CX717, though little data has been released, while tulrampator (S-47445) is an exception to the low-impact profile of most ampakines.[25]

Gary Lynch co-authored 1990s papers on facilitating glutamate receptors to enhance memory, including a 1994 study in PNAS, and the research led to Cortex's ampakine programme.[25] The military showed interest as well: Wikipedia cites 2008 reporting on a US military programme to reduce sleep need, and DARPA investigated ampakines for sleep-deprivation-induced cognitive decline.[25]

Per Wikipedia's account of the company, the FDA approved phase II trials of CX717 for Alzheimer's disease, ADHD and sleep disorders in February 2005, then halted CX717 trials over toxicity concerns in 2006, with testing later resuming at low doses. In July 2007 Alzheimer's trials were allowed to continue, but the FDA refused to let phase II ADHD trials proceed in September 2007, and German regulators approved studies of CX717 for opioid-induced breathing problems in March 2008.[26]
The company became RespireRx Pharmaceuticals in 2015. As of October 2025 none of its candidates had regulatory approval.[26] RespireRx holds patents covering most medical uses of the class.[25]

Ampakines bind an allosteric site on AMPA receptors and slow deactivation and desensitisation, lengthening synaptic currents and supporting long-term potentiation [2][2]. Lab work shows they can raise BDNF expression [10][11]. Low-impact types (CX516, CX1739) and high-impact types (CX717, farampator) are distinguished by how strongly they alter receptor kinetics [2][12].

Ampakines are discussed in nootropic communities as potential memory and alertness enhancers because of the 1990s memory work and the military sleep-deprivation research.[13][16] A 2009 German-language review discusses such compounds under the heading of neuro-enhancement or brain doping.[27] Ampakines remain investigational compounds, and the human literature does not include studies of cognitive enhancement in healthy young adults for study or training performance.

Early human work showed CX516 improved memory encoding in healthy older volunteers [13]. Schizophrenia add-on trials of CX516 reported little cognitive benefit [14][4][15]. CX717 reduced effects of sleep deprivation in monkeys [16] and showed promise in a 2025 adult ADHD trial [7]. CX1739 was tested for safety in healthy young volunteers [17]. Respiratory research examines ampakines for opioid-induced respiratory depression [9][18]. A 2025 Russian randomized trial examined ampakines for mixed anxiety-depressive disorder in the early period of ischemic stroke,[28] and a 2024 study reported site-specific analgesic effects in the cortex.[29]

Registered trials include CX516 with clozapine, olanzapine or risperidone (n=105) [19], CX717 in adult ADHD (n=68) [20], CX516 in fragile X syndrome and autism [21], and CX1739 for opioid respiratory depression [22]. Two depression studies of AMPA modulators were withdrawn or terminated [23][24].

Published human results. A placebo-controlled pilot study of CX516 added to antipsychotics in schizophrenia, a CX516 trial in elderly participants with mild cognitive impairment, a case series of CX516 as a single agent in schizophrenia, and a farampator study in healthy elderly volunteers are all listed above.[4][5][6][8] A Cochrane review of glutamatergic drugs for schizophrenia also covers this group.[14]

High-impact ampakines are described as having a narrower margin, with seizures reported at high doses in preclinical work [2]. Farampator has been associated with headache, drowsiness, nausea and impaired episodic memory.[25] Wikipedia notes that few side effects have been determined for the class.[25] Human safety data are limited to early-phase trials.

card.summary: Experimental AMPA-receptor boosters studied for memory, attention and alertness.

quick.overview:
Ampakines are research compounds that amplify glutamate signalling at AMPA receptors. People interested in focus and memory follow them as potential cognitive enhancers.

CX717 showed promise in a 2025 ADHD trial, while CX516 had mixed results in schizophrenia studies. No ampakine is approved.
quick.mechanism: They slow AMPA channel deactivation so each glutamate signal lasts longer, supporting plasticity and BDNF expression.
quick.risks: Investigational with limited human data; high-impact types carry seizure risk at high doses in preclinical work.
